I have been pondering about how to combine RGB laser beams for a while, and how to do this to get an evenly spread white beam when combined. My main concern is to try to get a grip on aspects like collimation, beam divergence, beam profile, chromatic aberration and such.

Until now I thought that getting control over the divergence, diameter and profile of the separate beams will let me get an evenly spread white beam. But then I stumbled upon this web page the other day where they treat the beam profile and astigmatism as different aspects of the light from a laser diode:

[http://laser.physics.sunysb.edu/~xueqin ... ort/p2.htm](http://laser.physics.sunysb.edu/~xueqing/webreport/p2.htm)

So now I am confused. It seems I need to control both beam profile (oval-circular) and astigmatism to get a nice even white beam after the spatial filter. Is there an optical physicist, or someone else, here that can explain this?

posts.topic_title: Measuring the astigmatism of a laser diode?
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Measuring the astigmatism of a laser diode?
posts.content_md:
> **DJ Mathson:** First I need some way to visualize what is going on; what does the original beam look like from the diode, what happens when the beam pass through the different optics and what will the profile look like on different distances due to the optics? I have a hard time trying to visualize this.

I have two aquariums just for this purpose. Take an aquarium of adequate size, and fill it with water. Then add a very small amount of colorant. I like to use a very tiny dab of white watercolor pigment, but you could probably use any number of different substances. The idea is to get a low concentration of light-reflecting particles in the water. It's important to add as little as possible, or else the laser light will be quickly absorbed, and won't pass through the aquarium. The colorant should be of such a low concentration that it won't be visible when looking at the water directly, but will be easily seen when the laser beam goes through the liquid. Then place your optics underwater, and direct the laser beam into the side of the aquarium and through the optics. The beam size and shape will be clearly visible in the tank. I don't know if this will solve your problem, but for people who haven't done it, it will definitely be a learning experience.

posts.content_md: My apologies - I was wrong. This is not just a diffraction phenomenon but involves the laser diode structure (index vs. gain guided) as described in this Melles Griot page [http://www.mellesgriot.com/pdf/corast.pdf](http://www.mellesgriot.com/pdf/corast.pdf) , which also describes a measurement technique. Don't know how significant it is for display holography, but I'll leave it to those with actual knowledge of the subject to comment further.
